traps.note: In SAS a missing payment_date counts as smaller than any date, so payment_date <= &as_of keeps rows with no date. A Spark filter drops them, so the translation needs an explicit isNull() OR.
&as_of is a SAS day count (days since 1960) compared with payment_date. In Spark it has to become a date literal, or the column has to be converted, before the comparison.

traps.snippet:
retain n_payments n_recoveries total_paid indemnity_amt expense_amt recovery_amt
         first_payment_date last_payment_date recovery_flag;
traps.note: The accumulators and the first/last dates are retained across rows and reset at first.claim_id. The result depends on the row order (claim_id, _row_seq), so Spark needs an ordered window or an aggregate.
first.claim_id resets the counters, and first_payment_date is the payment_date of the first row in _row_seq order, not the earliest date. Spark needs a window ordered by _row_seq.
The sum statement n_payments + 1 is implicitly retained and counts every row, including rows kept with a missing date.
The sum statement treats a missing amount as 0, so total_paid is never missing. In Spark this means a NULL-skipping F.sum or a coalesce.
The sum statement total_paid + amount is retained and accumulates in row order within the claim.

traps.snippet: if ptype = 'INDEMNITY' then indemnity_amt = indemnity_amt + amount;
traps.note: indemnity_amt = indemnity_amt + amount uses plain +, so one missing amount makes indemnity_amt missing for the rest of the claim. F.sum would skip the NULL and give a different result.

traps.snippet: else if ptype = 'EXPENSE' then expense_amt = expense_amt + amount;
traps.note: In expense_amt = expense_amt + amount, + propagates a missing amount for the rest of the claim. F.sum would not reproduce this.

traps.snippet: else if ptype = 'RECOVERY' then recovery_amt = recovery_amt + amount;
traps.note: In recovery_amt = recovery_amt + amount, + propagates a missing amount for the rest of the claim. F.sum would not reproduce this.
In SAS, amount < 0 is true when amount is missing, so a payment with no amount sets recovery_flag and adds to n_recoveries. A Spark when() treats it as false.
n_recoveries + 1 is retained and reset per claim. It is part of the carried state that has to become a conditional count.

traps.snippet:
last_payment_date = payment_date;
  if last.claim_id then output;
traps.note: last_payment_date is the payment_date of the last row in _row_seq order (not the maximum date), and it is output at last.claim_id. Spark needs a last value over a window ordered by _row_seq.
Latent: MERGE BY matches a missing claim_id with a missing claim_id, but a Spark equi-join never matches NULL keys. The translation would need a null-safe join if any keys are missing.
This MERGE with in= flags and 'if c' is a left join from claims to pay_summary. has_payment = p comes from the in= flag, and claims with no payments keep missing values in the pay_summary columns.
gross_paid uses +, so it is missing for claims with no payments (their indemnity_amt and expense_amt are not reset to 0) and for claims where an amount was missing. The translation must not coalesce.
sum() skips missing arguments and is missing only if all three are missing, so it is missing for claims with no payments. Spark needs coalesce logic that keeps NULL only when every argument is NULL.

defects.title: Split amounts, gross_paid and net_paid left missing for claims with no payments
defects.description: For claims with no payments (not p), the merge leaves indemnity_amt, expense_amt and recovery_amt missing. The not-p block (lines 96-101) only resets n_payments, n_recoveries, total_paid and recovery_flag. gross_paid uses '+' on missing values and net_paid is sum() of only missing values, so both come out missing instead of 0.
defects.intended_behaviour: CR-1873 keeps unpaid claims with explicit zeros. indemnity_amt, expense_amt and recovery_amt should be set to 0 in the not-p block, so that gross_paid and net_paid are 0.

defects.title: A missing payment amount wipes out the payment-type bucket for the rest of the claim
defects.description: total_paid uses the sum statement, which ignores missing values. The type split uses 'indemnity_amt = indemnity_amt + amount' (and the same for expense and recovery). One missing amount therefore makes that bucket missing, and it stays missing for every later payment on the claim. gross_paid and net_paid are then wrong as well.
defects.intended_behaviour: Add up the split the same way as total_paid, ignoring missing amounts (sum statement or sum()), so the bucket holds the sum of the amounts that are known.

defects.title: First and last payment dates taken from keying order, not from the dates
defects.description: Payments are sorted by claim_id and _row_seq (the order they were keyed). first_payment_date is the date on the first keyed row and last_payment_date is the date on the last keyed row. defects.title: Payments with a missing payment_date get past the reporting-date filter
defects.description: In SAS a missing date is lower than any value, so where=(payment_date <= &as_of) keeps payments with no date. Undated payments are counted in n_payments and total_paid, and the type split, and can make first_payment_date or last_payment_date missing.

defects.title: Recoveries identified by a negative amount, not by payment_type
defects.description: recovery_amt is built from payment_type = 'RECOVERY', but n_recoveries and recovery_flag count every negative amount. defects.intended_behaviour: Identify a recovery the same way recovery_amt does, i.e. payment_type = 'RECOVERY', so that n_recoveries, recovery_flag and recovery_amt agree.

defects.title: Duplicate claim_id on the register produces repeated output rows
defects.description: stg.claims is sorted without NODUPKEY, so any claim_id that appears more than once on the register comes out more than once, each copy carrying the same payment totals. risk_scoring.sas then counts that claim's paid amounts more than once.
defects.intended_behaviour: One row per claim: deduplicate the register (for example keep the latest _row_seq per claim_id) before the merge.

tests.description: Several payments have no amount (payment_date is NOT NULL, so the testable missing-value case is line 73). In SAS, amount < 0 is true when amount is missing, so those payments set recovery_flag=1 and add to n_recoveries. A naive F.when(amount < 0) treats NULL as false, so it gives recovery_flag 0 and undercounts n_recoveries. Claim 2 has a real negative recovery and claim 4 has only positive amounts, as the canonical cases. Claim 5 has no payments.

Payment dates sit on both sides of AsOfDate=2025-12-31: exactly on the date (kept), the day after (dropped), well after (dropped), and one before 1960-01-01, which is a negative SAS day count. If &as_of is left as a raw day count, or compared as a string or integer against a Spark date column, the wrong rows are kept or dropped. Claim 3 has only post-cutoff payments, so its has_payment should be 0.

Payments were keyed out of date order, and the rows of different claims are interleaved in _row_seq. The retained first_payment_date and last_payment_date take the dates of the first and last rows by (claim_id, _row_seq). They are not the min and max dates, which a naive aggregate would give. Claim 1 also has a post-cutoff row in the middle, which has to be filtered out before the ordering. The claims register is not sorted by claim_id. Claim 4 is the canonical case: its payments are in date order.

Some typed payments have a missing amount. The sum statement treats it as 0 in total_paid. But the plain + in indemnity_amt, expense_amt and recovery_amt makes that bucket missing for the rest of the claim, even after later non-missing payments. gross_paid (+) is then missing, while net_paid (sum()) skips the missing bucket. A naive F.sum skips the NULLs and gives non-null buckets and a non-null gross_paid. Claim 4 is the canonical case with no missing amounts. Claim 5 has no payments, so gross_paid and net_paid are missing and should not be coalesced.

The MERGE with in= flags and 'if c' is a left join from the register. Claims 3 and 5 have no payments, and claim 6 has only payments after the cutoff. All three must be kept with has_payment=0, the four counters set to 0, and indemnity/expense/recovery/gross/net left missing. Claim 99 has payments but is not on the register, so it must be dropped. A naive inner join, a full join, coalescing every column to 0, or deriving has_payment from n_payments>0 would differ. Claims 1, 2 and 4 are matched as the canonical case.

It does not drop claim rows: every claim on stg.claims appears in the output because of `if c`. first_payment_date and last_payment_date come from the first and last payment in _row_seq (keying) order, not the earliest and latest payment_date. If payments were keyed out of date order, the two can differ from MIN and MAX. For claims with no payments (not p), n_payments, n_recoveries, total_paid and recovery_flag are set to 0. indemnity_amt, expense_amt, recovery_amt and the payment dates are left missing, so gross_paid is missing too (+ on missing values gives missing). net_paid uses sum() and is also missing when all three amounts are missing. Watch for this in the PySpark port. Also, gross_paid is missing for a paid claim whose payments are all one type (for example indemnity only), because the other amount stays 0 there, not missing. In fact both amounts start at 0 for every paid claim, so gross_paid is only missing for claims with no payments. Payment types other than INDEMNITY, EXPENSE and RECOVERY count toward total_paid but toward no split column. n_recoveries and recovery_flag depend on the sign of amount, not on payment_type.

warnings:
translator notes: 1. The running sums use ordered windows from the first row to the current one, partitioned by claim_id and ordered by _row_seq. This keeps the legacy order of double additions. The last row per claim (row_number descending) is the last.claim_id output.
2. The type buckets start at 0 and add up the amounts of their type, skipping nulls. A flag turns a bucket NULL if any of its rows had a missing amount, which reproduces how + propagates a missing value through a retained variable.
3. The merge is a left join that uses eqNullSafe, so a missing claim_id matches a missing claim_id the way MERGE BY does (the latent SAS-01 finding). pay_summary is unique per claim_id, so duplicate claims rows each get the same summary, as in the legacy one-to-many merge.
4. net_paid uses coalesce(x, 0) and differs from SAS sum() only in the sign of a zero (-0.0 versus 0.0). That cannot happen with decimal amounts.
5. F.upper is Unicode-aware and SAS upcase may not be. They agree on ASCII lob_code and status values.
6. claim_number is right-trimmed, and blank values become NULL.
